# Managed Provider MCP additions

These commands are separate from read-only `provider mcp-preview`:

```text
loeyae-aidlc provider mcp-plan --project <project> --host-config <explicit.json> [--host-domains <domains.json>]
loeyae-aidlc provider mcp-apply --project <project> --host-config <explicit.json> --plan <saved-plan.json> --approve-config <sha256:digest> [--approve-config <sha256:digest> ...] [--host-domains <domains.json>]
```

Save the JSON output of `mcp-plan` as UTF-8. Review each requirement in its immutable cached Manifest and supply each approved `changes[].config_digest` independently to apply. A plan or preview never supplies execution permission. Changing a command, arguments, environment, URL or headers requires a different approved digest. Host applications may automatically execute newly added configurations when they next read this file; approve only configurations whose execution you intend to allow. Neither command executes a Provider, MCP server, package script or network request, or expands credentials.

The initial target format is a regular JSON object containing `mcpServers`. The caller must name the target file again when applying; parents must already exist. A missing target means an empty configuration. No discovery of real host files or TOML conversion is performed. Removal uses the separate explicit cleanup commands below. Unknown host fields and existing compatible entries remain intact, including untyped stdio representation. Pin, autoApprove, disabled, configuration and credential-domain differences reject the operation.

The versioned `aidlc.mcp-plan/v2` binds the canonical target, its byte digest, structure, optional domain-file digest, ledger digest, complete project intent/immutable lock digest, individual source provenance, domains and add/reuse decisions. Config values and host secrets are omitted. The stable project consumer is a digest of its canonical real directory, independent of the current Provider set or Git branch. Moving a project intentionally creates a new consumer; existing records remain available for a later explicit reconciliation. Apply recalculates the plan inside the target lock and rejects drift, unknown versions and fields. A successful plan may be replayed unchanged only when its receipt, current managed references, source, domains and resulting host bytes still match. Cleanup revokes this project’s prior receipts. Otherwise re-plan.

The initial safety policy accepts basename stdio commands and a restricted argument alphabet (no spaces, shell expressions, or credential-like flags), and HTTPS transports without credentials, fragments or query parameters. Every environment/header value must be a literal controlled `${env:UPPER_CASE_NAME}` reference. This syntax must be supported by the selected host; Core does not resolve it. Credentials belong in the host's environment, never literal Provider metadata. Exact digest approval remains required for reuse and addition. The policy is intentionally narrow; unsupported shapes reject rather than being rewritten.

`credential_domain` is an attribution identifier, never a credential or authentication result. New entries record the declared domain. External reuse of any domain other than `none` needs a matching explicit `--host-domains` map; external entries remain externally owned. Managed entries obtain attribution from their ledger. Different domains cannot share a name. Already managed compatible reuse records the additional project consumer and immutable source references without changing configuration. No Provider, only disabled instances, or exclusively external compatible reuse creates no configuration or ledger.

For `host.json`, shared transaction files live beside it:

- `host.json.aidlc-mcp-lock`: one exclusive file lock across all cooperating projects, containing the writer PID. Busy writers fail and can re-plan/retry after completion. A crashed process can leave this lock: verify its PID is no longer running before an operator removes this file. Locks are never stolen based on age, which could admit two live writers.
- `host.json.aidlc-mcp-ledger.json`: `aidlc.mcp-ownership/v2`, containing target/entry, original consumer, all known managed consumers, Provider instance/lock provenance, before/after entry fingerprints, credential domain, transaction identifier and committed state. Only newly added entries receive ownership; external reuse is never adopted. No config values are stored.
- `host.json.aidlc-mcp-journal.json`: `aidlc.mcp-transaction/v2`, containing the plan, before/after host digests and baseline/intended metadata. A prepared ledger records the plan and journal digests before configuration publication; the journal alone grants no ownership authority. Journal, host and ledger use temporary exclusive files, fsync and atomic replacement. These sidecars are local operational state, not shared Provider source artifacts; keep them with the host configuration and exclude them from source control.

After interruption, rerun apply with the original plan, explicit target/domain file and approvals. If a configuration-changing transaction still has its before bytes, recovery rolls back the prepare metadata and rejects with an instruction to re-plan. A metadata-only transaction can complete directly. If it has the exact after bytes, finish only the metadata publication. If host or ledger bytes differ, preserve them and report a recovery conflict. No recovery replays a saved full host configuration, and the journal contains no host secrets. Recovery itself can be interrupted and resumed. Metadata-only consumer updates follow the same journal protocol. Pending transactions from another plan must first be resolved with their original inputs.

The lock/CAS protects cooperating local writers and detects host edits before publication. It does not promise exclusion against an unrelated program replacing a directory or writing in the final check-to-rename interval; coordinate host editors during apply. Symlinks/junctions in target ancestry, hardlinked files, traversal, source-state targets and linked sidecars are rejected. Process interruption recovery is covered; filesystem/hardware power-loss guarantees depend on the operating system. An unresolved conflict or orphan lock requires operator attention, never automatic deletion of user configuration.

## Explicit cleanup and project release

```text
loeyae-aidlc provider mcp-cleanup-plan --project <project> --host-config <explicit.json> [--host-domains <domains.json>] [--release-all]
loeyae-aidlc provider mcp-cleanup --project <project> --host-config <explicit.json> --plan <saved-cleanup.json> [--host-domains <domains.json>] [--release-all]
```

Review the JSON plan before execution; repeat the explicit target, domains and release mode. These commands never execute MCP processes. Disable/remove only return a cleanup hint; they do not scan or edit host files. Normal cleanup releases this canonical project’s references whose names are no longer needed by any enabled Provider. Remaining Provider provenance is refreshed without removing the reference. Unknown requirements block normal cleanup. `--release-all` explicitly releases all registered references for this project even while Providers remain enabled. Other projects and moved/missing project directories are never inferred to have exited.

The `aidlc.mcp-cleanup-plan/v1` binds the project, release mode, effective intent/lock, target bytes, domains, baseline ledger state, entry ownership fingerprints and remaining consumers. Execution recomputes under the same target lock as apply. Another consumer retains the entry. Only a final consumer of a committed, mechanism-created entry with an exact current entry fingerprint and matching domain attribution can delete that entry. Other server entries, host settings and the config file itself remain. Without an explicit domain map the committed ledger supplies attribution; a supplied map must explicitly match the entry’s domain.

User edits (including env, pin, approval and disabled fields), missing entries, prior conflicts and unknown/changed domain attribution return explicit reasons. Releasing these references preserves host bytes and marks the ownership record `retained`, even if other consumers remain. Its original fingerprint is never refreshed. This tombstone prevents subsequent cleanup or apply from silently deleting or adopting the entry, even if its original configuration is later restored. Manual reconciliation is required; deleting this metadata is not an automatic cleanup procedure. External reuse has no managed reference and remains untouched.

Cleanup shares v2 preparation, atomic publication and recovery with apply, including metadata-only releases. Interrupted recovery never rewrites saved host bytes. Rerun the original command/plan; later host, source, domain or ledger edits block recovery. A journal without a matching current prepare anchor or exact completed ledger cannot grant permission. All persisted snapshots contain metadata and digests, not host configurations or secrets.

Compatibility: v1 ownership ledgers are read conservatively and upgraded on the next actual transaction. v1 apply plans are rejected; produce a fresh v2 plan. Unresolved v1 journals are rejected by this version: resolve them with the original v1 implementation and approvals before upgrading; never delete a pending journal to bypass recovery. Core installation and upgrades deploy workflow entries and Hooks without domain MCP defaults; --project is deployment scope, never connection approval. Historical host entries are preserved without adoption or migration. Uninstall does not release managed MCP references. Other host formats remain future increments.

## After Core installation

Installation never runs these commands automatically. With no Provider or only disabled instances there are no connections; missing aidlc.mcp metadata is a capability gap, not permission to infer defaults. Use the preview/plan/apply commands above only for enabled, immutably locked requirements and an explicit target. Review and approve every configuration digest; repeat --approve-config for multiple changes. Save JSON plans as UTF-8 (Windows PowerShell 5.1 redirection defaults to UTF-16; select UTF-8 explicitly).

This adapter supports JSON mcpServers (for example an explicitly selected Kiro or Qoder host file). It does not map ZCode mcp.servers, plugin-managed declarations or Codex/OpenCode configuration. Do not apply directly to those files. Qoder CN bridge recipes must be provided by locked Provider metadata and explicitly approved; Core does not generate or start a bridge. Host authentication remains a separate host operation.
